claim: The CovILD study is a longitudinal, multicenter observational study in ambulatory and hospitalized COVID-19 patients recruited in early 2020 with n = 145 participants.
source: We conducted a longitudinal, multicenter observational study in ambulatory and hospitalized COVID-19 patients recruited in early 2020 (n = 145).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the study design, type, and sample size in the Methods section.

claim: At the 6-month follow-up, 49% of participants reported persistent symptoms.
source: At the 6-month follow-up, 49% of participants reported persistent symptoms.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding in the Results section of the abstract.

claim: The frequency of structural lung CT abnormalities ranged from 18% in the mild outpatient cases to 76% in the intensive care unit (ICU) convalescents.
source: The frequency of structural lung CT abnormalities ranged from 18% in the mild outpatient cases to 76% in the intensive care unit (ICU) convalescents.
evidence: This is a direct statement of study findings in the Results section of the abstract.

claim: Prevalence of impaired LF ranged from 14% in the mild outpatient cases to 50% in the ICU survivors.
source: Prevalence of impaired LF ranged from 14% in the mild outpatient cases to 50% in the ICU survivors.
evidence: This is a direct statement of study findings in the Results section of the abstract.

claim: Incomplete radiological lung recovery was associated with increased anti-S1/S2 antibody titer, IL-6, and CRP levels at the early follow-up.
source: Incomplete radiological lung recovery was associated with increased anti-S1/S2 antibody titer, IL-6, and CRP levels at the early follow-up.
evidence: This is a direct statement of an association finding in the Results section of the abstract.

claim: The risk of perturbed pulmonary recovery could be robustly estimated at early follow-up by clustering and machine learning classifiers employing solely non-CT and non-LF parameters.
source: We demonstrated that the risk of perturbed pulmonary recovery could be robustly estimated at early follow-up by clustering and machine learning classifiers employing solely non-CT and non-LF parameters.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding in the Results section of the abstract.

claim: The severity of acute COVID-19 and protracted systemic inflammation is strongly linked to persistent structural and functional lung abnormality.
source: The severity of acute COVID-19 and protracted systemic inflammation is strongly linked to persistent structural and functional lung abnormality.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study conclusion in the Conclusions section of the abstract.

claim: As of December 2021, the John Hopkins dashboard reports 276 million cases and 5.4 million COVID-19-related deaths worldwide.
source: As of December 2021, the John Hopkins dashboard (Dong et al., 2020)⁠ reports 276 million cases and 5.4 million COVID-19-related deaths worldwide (Johns Hopkins Coronavirus Resource Center, 2021)⁠.
evidence: This statement cites external sources for COVID-19 case and death statistics.

claim: Approximately 10–15% of COVID-19 cases progress to a severe condition and approximately 5% suffer from critical illness.
source: Although the vast majority of COVID-19 patients display mild disease, approximately 10–15% of cases progress to a severe condition and approximately 5% suffer from critical illness (Perez-Saez, 2021; Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement cites published literature for COVID-19 severity statistics.

claim: Similar to severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), a significant portion of COVID-19 patients report lingering or recurring clinical impairment and cardiopulmonary recovery may take several months to years.
source: Similar to severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) (Hui et al., 2005; Ng et al., 2004; Ngai et al., 2010; Lam et al., 2009)⁠, a significant portion of COVID-19 patients report lingering or recurring clinical impairment and cardiopulmonary recovery may take several months to years (Sonnweber et al., 2021; Sahanic et al., 2021; Caruso et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021b; Huang et al., 2021a; Faverio et al., 2021; Hellemons et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021; Venkatesan, 2021)⁠.
evidence: This statement cites multiple published studies comparing COVID-19 recovery to SARS.

claim: The term 'long COVID' is defined by the persistence of COVID-19 symptoms for more than 4 weeks.
source: This observation has led to the introduction of the term 'long COVID,' defined by the persistence of COVID-19 symptoms for more than 4 weeks, and the 'post-acute sequelae of COVID-19' (PASC) referring to symptom persistence for more than 12 weeks (Sahanic et al., 2021; Shah et al., 2021; Sudre et al., 2021b)⁠.
evidence: This statement cites published literature for the definition of 'long COVID'.

claim: The 'post-acute sequelae of COVID-19' (PASC) refers to symptom persistence for more than 12 weeks.
source: This observation has led to the introduction of the term 'long COVID,' defined by the persistence of COVID-19 symptoms for more than 4 weeks, and the 'post-acute sequelae of COVID-19' (PASC) referring to symptom persistence for more than 12 weeks (Sahanic et al., 2021; Shah et al., 2021; Sudre et al., 2021b)⁠.
evidence: This statement cites published literature for the definition of PASC.

claim: Follow-up investigations were performed at 60 days (63 ± 23 days [mean ± SD]), 100 days (103 ± 21 days), and 180 days (190 ± 15 days) after diagnosis of COVID-19.
source: We retrospectively assessed patient characteristics during acute COVID-19 and performed follow-up investigations at 60 days (63 ± 23 days [mean ± SD]; visit 1), 100 days (103 ± 21 days; visit 2), and 180 days (190 ± 15 days; visit 3) after diagnosis of COVID-19.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study follow-up schedule.

claim: Impaired LF was defined as (1) forced vital capacity (FVC) < 80% or (2) forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) < 80%, or (3) FEV1:FVC < 70% or (4) total lung capacity (TLC) < 80% or (5) diffusing capacity of carbon monoxide (DLCO) < 80% predicted.
source: Impaired LF was defined as (1) forced vital capacity (FVC) < 80% or (2) forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) < 80%, or (3) FEV1:FVC < 70% or (4) total lung capacity (TLC) < 80% or (5) diffusing capacity of carbon monoxide (DLCO) < 80% predicted.
evidence: This is a direct statement defining the criteria for impaired lung function.

claim: Most patients, irrespective of the acute COVID-19 severity, showed a significant resolution of disease symptoms over time.
source: Most patients, irrespective of the acute COVID-19 severity, showed a significant resolution of disease symptoms over time (Figure 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in figures showing symptom resolution over time.

claim: Self-reported impaired physical performance (34.7%), sleep disorders (27.1%), and exertional dyspnea (22.8%) were the leading manifestations of persistent complaints at the 6-month follow-up.
source: Persistent complaints at the 6-month follow-up were reported by 49% of the study subjects (Table 3), with self-reported impaired physical performance (34.7%), sleep disorders (27.1%), and exertional dyspnea (22.8%) as leading manifestations.
evidence: This is a direct statement of study findings regarding persistent symptoms.

claim: The frequency of all investigated symptoms declined significantly, even though the pace of their resolution was remarkably slower in the late (100- and 180-day follow-ups) than in the early recovery phase (acute COVID-19 till 60-day follow-up).
source: The frequency of all investigated symptoms declined significantly, even though the pace of their resolution was remarkably slower in the late (100- and 180-day follow-ups) than in the early recovery phase (acute COVID-19 till 60-day follow-up) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2B showing symptom resolution kinetics.

claim: Except for the critical COVID-19 survivors (60 days: 66.7%; 180 days post-COVID-19: 50%), no significant reduction in the frequency of LF impairment over time was observed.
source: Except for the critical COVID-19 survivors (60 days: 66.7%; 180 days post-COVID-19: 50%), no significant reduction in the frequency of LF impairment over time was observed (Figure 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3 showing lung function recovery kinetics.

claim: The majority of the participants with impaired LF displayed radiological lung findings.
source: The majority of the participants with impaired LF displayed radiological lung findings.
evidence: This is a direct statement of an observed relationship between lung function and CT findings.

claim: A substantial fraction of CT abnormalities, especially mild ones, were accompanied neither by persistent symptoms nor by LF deficits.
source: However, a substantial fraction of CT abnormalities, especially mild ones, were accompanied neither by persistent symptoms nor by LF deficits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in supplementary figures showing overlap between outcomes.

claim: The frequency, scoring, and recovery of CT lung findings were related to the severity of acute infection.
source: The frequency, scoring, and recovery of CT lung findings were related to the severity of acute infection.
evidence: This is a direct statement of an observed relationship between acute COVID-19 severity and CT findings.

claim: Pulmonary lesions scored > 5 CT severity points at the 180-day follow-up were most frequent in the individuals with severe and critical acute COVID-19.
source: Pulmonary lesions scored > 5 CT severity points at the 180-day follow-up were most frequent in the individuals with severe and critical acute COVID-19 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The hospitalized group with oxygen therapy demonstrated the fastest recovery kinetics.
source: Notably, the hospitalized group with oxygen therapy demonstrated the fastest recovery kinetics.
evidence: This is a direct statement of an observed pattern in recovery kinetics.

claim: LF and CT lung recovery decelerated in the late phase of COVID-19 convalescence.
source: As for the symptom resolution, LF and CT lung recovery decelerated in the late phase of COVID-19 convalescence (Figure 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3 showing recovery kinetics.

claim: No significant correlates for long-term symptom persistence were identified by univariate modeling of 52 binary clinical parameters.
source: By this means, no significant correlates for long-term symptom persistence were identified.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a negative finding from univariate risk modeling.

claim: Risk factors and readouts of severe and critical COVID-19 including multimorbidity, malignancy, male sex, prolonged hospitalization, ICU stay, and immunosuppressive therapy were significantly associated with persistent CT abnormalities.
source: Risk factors and readouts of severe and critical COVID-19 including multimorbidity, malignancy, male sex, prolonged hospitalization, ICU stay, and immunosuppressive therapy were significantly associated with persistent CT (Figure 4) and LF abnormalities (Figure 5).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figures 4 and 5 showing risk factors.

claim: Risk factors and readouts of severe and critical COVID-19 including multimorbidity, malignancy, male sex, prolonged hospitalization, ICU stay, and immunosuppressive therapy were significantly associated with persistent LF abnormalities.
source: Risk factors and readouts of severe and critical COVID-19 including multimorbidity, malignancy, male sex, prolonged hospitalization, ICU stay, and immunosuppressive therapy were significantly associated with persistent CT (Figure 4) and LF abnormalities (Figure 5).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figures 4 and 5 showing risk factors.

claim: Persistently elevated inflammatory markers, IL-6 (>7 ng/L) and CRP (>0.5 mg/L), were strong unfavorable risk factors for incomplete radiological and functional pulmonary recovery.
source: Persistently elevated inflammatory markers, IL-6 (>7 ng/L) and CRP (>0.5 mg/L), were strong unfavorable risk factors for incomplete radiological and functional pulmonary recovery.
evidence: This is a direct statement of risk factors identified in the study.

claim: The biochemical readout of microvascular inflammation, D-dimer (>500 pg/mL) was significantly linked to LF deficits.
source: Additionally, the biochemical readout of microvascular inflammation, D-dimer (>500 pg/mL) was significantly linked to LF deficits.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a risk factor identified in the study.

claim: Low serum anti-S1/S2 IgG titers at the 60-day follow-up and ambulatory acute COVID-19 correlated with an improved pulmonary recovery.
source: Low serum anti-S1/S2 IgG titers at the 60-day follow-up and ambulatory acute COVID-19 correlated with an improved pulmonary recovery (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figures 4 and 5 showing protective factors.

claim: Three clusters of co-occurring non-CT and non-LF clinical features of acute COVID-19 and early convalescence were identified using the unsupervised PAM algorithm.
source: Employing the unsupervised PAM algorithm (Amato et al., 2019)⁠, three clusters of co-occurring non-CT and non-LF clinical features of acute COVID-19 and early convalescence (Appendix 1—table 1) were identified (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Appendix 1—table 3): (1) cluster 1 with male sex, hypertension, and cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity; (2) cluster 2, including characteristics of acute COVID-19 severity and inflammatory markers; and (3) cluster 3 consisting of acute and persistent COVID-19 symptoms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This statement describes the clustering analysis results with reference to figures and tables.

claim: Cluster 1 included male sex, hypertension, and cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity.
source: Employing the unsupervised PAM algorithm (Amato et al., 2019)⁠, three clusters of co-occurring non-CT and non-LF clinical features of acute COVID-19 and early convalescence (Appendix 1—table 1) were identified (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Appendix 1—table 3): (1) cluster 1 with male sex, hypertension, and cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity; (2) cluster 2, including characteristics of acute COVID-19 severity and inflammatory markers; and (3) cluster 3 consisting of acute and persistent COVID-19 symptoms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This statement describes the composition of cluster 1 from the clustering analysis.

claim: Cluster 2 included characteristics of acute COVID-19 severity and inflammatory markers.
source: Employing the unsupervised PAM algorithm (Amato et al., 2019)⁠, three clusters of co-occurring non-CT and non-LF clinical features of acute COVID-19 and early convalescence (Appendix 1—table 1) were identified (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Appendix 1—table 3): (1) cluster 1 with male sex, hypertension, and cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity; (2) cluster 2, including characteristics of acute COVID-19 severity and inflammatory markers; and (3) cluster 3 consisting of acute and persistent COVID-19 symptoms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This statement describes the composition of cluster 2 from the clustering analysis.

claim: Cluster 3 consisted of acute and persistent COVID-19 symptoms.
source: Employing the unsupervised PAM algorithm (Amato et al., 2019)⁠, three clusters of co-occurring non-CT and non-LF clinical features of acute COVID-19 and early convalescence (Appendix 1—table 1) were identified (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Appendix 1—table 3): (1) cluster 1 with male sex, hypertension, and cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity; (2) cluster 2, including characteristics of acute COVID-19 severity and inflammatory markers; and (3) cluster 3 consisting of acute and persistent COVID-19 symptoms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This statement describes the composition of cluster 3 from the clustering analysis.

claim: Long-term symptom persistence was associated with acute and long-lasting COVID-19 symptoms in cluster 3.
source: Long-term symptom persistence was associated with acute and long-lasting COVID-19 symptoms in cluster 3, whereas pulmonary outcome parameters were grouped with cluster 2 features (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This statement describes the association between outcome variables and feature clusters.

claim: Pulmonary outcome parameters were grouped with cluster 2 features.
source: Long-term symptom persistence was associated with acute and long-lasting COVID-19 symptoms in cluster 3, whereas pulmonary outcome parameters were grouped with cluster 2 features (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This statement describes the association between outcome variables and feature clusters.

claim: Preexisting comorbidities such as malignancy, kidney, lung and gastrointestinal disease, obesity, and diabetes were found the closest cluster neighbors of mild CT abnormalities (severity score ≤ 5).
source: Preexisting comorbidities such as malignancy, kidney, lung and gastrointestinal disease, obesity, and diabetes were found the closest cluster neighbors of mild CT abnormalities (severity score ≤ 5).
evidence: This statement describes the nearest neighbors of mild CT abnormalities in the feature clustering.

claim: Moderate-to-severe structural alterations (severity score > 5) and LF deficits were tightly linked to markers of protracted systemic inflammation (IL-6, CRP, anemia of inflammation).
source: Moderate-to-severe structural alterations (severity score > 5) and LF deficits were, in turn, tightly linked to markers of protracted systemic inflammation (IL-6, CRP, anemia of inflammation) (Sonnweber et al., 2020;⁠ Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement describes the nearest neighbors of moderate-to-severe CT abnormalities and LF deficits in the feature clustering.

claim: Three clusters of study participants were identified using a combined SOM – hierarchical clustering approach.
source: Applying a combined SOM – hierarchical clustering approach, three clusters of the study participants were identified (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Vesanto and Alhoniemi, 2000; Kohonen, 1995)⁠.
evidence: This statement describes the participant clustering analysis with reference to figures and citations.

claim: Prolonged hospitalization, anti-infective therapy, overweight or obesity, pain during acute COVID-19, and low anti-S1/S2 titers at the 60-day follow-up were found the most influential clustering features.
source: Prolonged hospitalization, anti-infective therapy, overweight or obesity, pain during acute COVID-19, and low anti-S1/S2 titers at the 60-day follow-up were found the most influential clustering features (Figure 7—figure supplement 2; Breiman, 2001)⁠.
evidence: This statement describes the most important features for participant clustering with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: The patient subsets identified by the SOM approach differed significantly in frequency of radiological lung abnormalities at the 180-day follow-up.
source: The patient subsets identified by the SOM approach differed significantly in frequency of radiological lung abnormalities and substantially, yet not significantly, in the frequency of LF impairment at the 180-day follow-up.
evidence: This statement describes the differences in outcomes between participant clusters.

claim: The patient subsets identified by the SOM approach differed substantially, yet not significantly, in the frequency of LF impairment at the 180-day follow-up.
source: The patient subsets identified by the SOM approach differed significantly in frequency of radiological lung abnormalities and substantially, yet not significantly, in the frequency of LF impairment at the 180-day follow-up.
evidence: This statement describes the differences in outcomes between participant clusters.

claim: Most of the individuals assigned to the largest, low-risk (LR) subset were CT and LF abnormality-free.
source: In particular, most of the individuals assigned to the largest, low-risk (LR) subset were CT and LF abnormality-free.
evidence: This statement describes the characteristics of the low-risk participant cluster.

claim: The frequency and severity of radiological pulmonary findings were elevated in the smallest intermediate-risk subset (IR) and peaked in the high-risk (HR) group.
source: The frequency and severity of radiological pulmonary findings were elevated in the smallest intermediate-risk subset (IR) and peaked in the high-risk (HR) group (Figure 8A).
evidence: This statement describes the characteristics of the intermediate-risk and high-risk participant clusters.

claim: Despite a comparable frequency of long-term symptoms between the LR, IR, and HR subsets, the HR collective showed the lowest prevalence of dyspnea, cough, night sweating, pain, gastrointestinal manifestations, and complete absence of hyposmia at the 180-day follow-up.
source: Despite a comparable frequency of long-term symptoms between the LR, IR, and HR subsets (Figure 8A), the HR collective showed the lowest prevalence of dyspnea, cough, night sweating, pain, gastrointestinal manifestations, and complete absence of hyposmia at the 180-day follow-up (Figure 8B).
evidence: This statement describes the symptom profiles of the participant clusters.

claim: Although the LR subset primarily comprised mild COVID-19 cases and the HR subset ICU survivors, the cluster assignment (IR vs. LR, HR vs. LR) remained an independent correlate of persistent CT and LF abnormalities after adjustment for the acute COVID-19 severity.
source: Although the LR subset primarily comprised mild COVID-19 cases and the HR subset ICU survivors, the cluster assignment (IR vs. LR, HR vs. LR) remained an independent correlate of persistent CT and LF abnormalities after adjustment for the acute COVID-19 severity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement describes the independence of cluster assignment from acute COVID-19 severity in predicting outcomes.

claim: All tested ML algorithms and ensembles demonstrated good accuracy (area under the curve [AUC] > 0.78) and sensitivity (>0.84) at predicting any lung CT abnormalities at the 6-month follow-up in the study cohort serving as a training data set.
source: All tested ML algorithms and ensembles demonstrated good accuracy (area under the curve [AUC] > 0.78) and sensitivity (>0.84) at predicting any lung CT abnormalities at the 6-month follow-up in the study cohort serving as a training data set.
evidence: This statement describes the performance of ML classifiers in the training cohort.

claim: The efficiency of ML algorithms and ensembles at predicting any lung CT abnormalities in CV was moderate (AUC: 0.69–0.81; sensitivity: 0.69–0.78).
source: Their efficiency in CV was moderate (AUC: 0.69–0.81; sensitivity: 0.69–0.78) (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 3, Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This statement describes the performance of ML classifiers in cross-validation.

claim: Moderate-to-severe structural lung findings were recognized with markedly lower sensitivity both in the training data set (>0.43) and the CV (0.39–0.48).
source: In turn, moderate-to-severe structural lung findings were recognized with markedly lower sensitivity both in the training data set (>0.43) and the CV (0.39–0.48).
evidence: This statement describes the performance of ML classifiers at predicting moderate-to-severe CT abnormalities.

claim: Nearly half of the cases of impaired LF and persistent symptoms were not identified by any of the tested ML algorithms and their ensembles in the CV setting.
source: Even though impaired LF and persistent symptoms were common at the 6-month follow-up in the training data set (Figures 2 and 3), nearly half of the cases were not identified by any of the tested ML algorithms and their ensembles in the CV setting (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 3, Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This statement describes the limited sensitivity of ML classifiers at predicting LF impairment and persistent symptoms.

claim: The sensitivity of the ensembles and single classifiers at predicting CT and LF abnormalities was substantially better in severe and critical COVID-19 survivors than in ambulatory and moderate cases.
source: The sensitivity of the ensembles and single classifiers at predicting CT and LF abnormalities was substantially better in severe and critical COVID-19 survivors than in ambulatory and moderate cases (Figure 10, Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This statement describes the differential performance of ML classifiers across severity groups.

claim: The most important explanatory variables for pulmonary abnormalities by three unrelated classifiers (C5.0, RF, and glmNet) included preexisting malignancy, multimorbidity, markers of systemic inflammation (IL-6 and CRP), and anti-S1/S2 antibody levels at the 60-day follow-up.
source: The most important explanatory variables for pulmonary abnormalities by three unrelated classifiers (C5.0, RF, and glmNet) included preexisting malignancy, multimorbidity, markers of systemic inflammation (IL-6 and CRP), and anti-S1/S2 antibody levels at the 60-day follow-up (Figure 9—figure supplement 4, Figure 9—figure supplement 5, Figure 9—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This statement describes the most important features identified by ML classifiers for predicting pulmonary abnormalities.

claim: The highly influential parameters at prediction of symptoms at the 180-day follow-up encompassed symptom presence at the 60-day follow-up, as well as obesity and dyspnea during acute COVID-19.
source: The highly influential parameters at prediction of symptoms at the 180-day follow-up encompassed symptom presence at the 60-day follow-up, as well as obesity and dyspnea during acute COVID-19 (Figure 9—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This statement describes the most important features identified by ML classifiers for predicting persistent symptoms.

claim: Despite the resolution of symptoms and pulmonary abnormalities at the 6-month follow-up in a large fraction of the study participants, the recovery pace was substantially slower in the late convalescence when compared with the first three months after diagnosis.
source: Despite the resolution of symptoms and pulmonary abnormalities at the 6-month follow-up in a large fraction of the study participants, the recovery pace was substantially slower in the late convalescence when compared with the first three months after diagnosis (Sonnweber et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021a)⁠.
evidence: This statement summarizes a key finding of the study with supporting citations.

claim: Persistent symptoms and CT findings were detected in more than 40% and reduced LF in approximately one-third of the cohort, which is in line with recovery kinetics and signs of lung lesion chronicity reported by others.
source: Persistent symptoms and CT findings were detected in more than 40% and reduced LF in approximately one-third of the cohort, which is in line with recovery kinetics and signs of lung lesion chronicity reported by others (Caruso et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021b; Huang et al., 2021a; Faverio et al., 2021; Hellemons et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021)⁠.
evidence: This statement summarizes a key finding of the study and compares it to published literature.

claim: Similar protracted pulmonary recovery was reported for SARS and non-COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome.
source: By comparison, similar protracted pulmonary recovery was reported for SARS (Hui et al., 2005; Ng et al., 2004; Ngai et al., 2010; Lam et al., 2009)⁠ and non-COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome (Wilcox et al., 2013; Masclans et al., 2011)⁠.
evidence: This statement cites published literature comparing COVID-19 recovery to other respiratory conditions.

claim: Treatment approaches for hospitalized patients in cohorts recruited at the pandemic onset in early 2020 differ significantly from the current standard of care for acute COVID-19, which includes early systemic steroid use and antiviral and various immunomodulatory medications.
source: Of note, treatment approaches for hospitalized patients in our cohorts and similar cohorts recruited at the pandemic onset in early 2020 (Caruso et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021b; Huang et al., 2021a; Faverio et al., 2021; Hellemons et al., 2021)⁠ differ significantly from the current standard of care for acute COVID-19, which includes early systemic steroid use and antiviral and various immunomodulatory medications.
evidence: This statement compares treatment approaches between early 2020 and current standards with supporting citations.

claim: In roughly half of study participants with abnormal lung CT findings, and especially in those with low-grade structural abnormalities, no overt LF impairment at follow-up was discerned.
source: In roughly half of our study participants with abnormal lung CT findings, and especially in those with low-grade structural abnormalities, no overt LF impairment at follow-up was discerned.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding regarding the relationship between CT findings and lung function.

claim: Even subclinical lung alterations may bear the potential for clinically relevant progression of interstitial lung disease requiring systematic CT and LF monitoring.
source: Still, even subclinical lung alterations may bear the potential for clinically relevant progression of interstitial lung disease (Suliman et al., 2015; Hatabu et al., 2020) requiring systematic CT and LF monitoring.
evidence: This statement cites published literature to support the clinical significance of subclinical lung alterations.

claim: Symptom persistence was weakly associated with incomplete functional or structural pulmonary recovery.
source: Conversely, symptom persistence was weakly associated with incomplete functional or structural pulmonary recovery.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding regarding the relationship between symptoms and pulmonary recovery.

claim: PASC are found in as many as 10% of COVID-19 patients.
source: Since PASC are found in as many as 10% of COVID-19 patients (Sahanic et al., 2021; Venkatesan, 2021; Sudre et al., 2021b)⁠, robust, resource-saving tools assessing the individual risk of pulmonary complications are urgently needed (Shah et al., 2021; Raghu and Wilson, 2020)⁠.
evidence: This statement cites published literature for the prevalence of PASC.

claim: Covariates and characteristics of severe acute COVID-19 such as male sex, age, and preexisting comorbidities, hospitalization, ventilation, and ICU stay were proposed as the risk factors of persistent pulmonary impairment.
source: Covariates and characteristics of severe acute COVID-19 such as male sex, age, and preexisting comorbidities, hospitalization, ventilation, and ICU stay were proposed as the risk factors of persistent pulmonary impairment (Sonnweber et al., 2021; Caruso et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021a; Faverio et al., 2021; Raghu and Wilson, 2020)⁠.
evidence: This statement cites published literature for previously proposed risk factors.

claim: The applicability of covariates and characteristics of severe acute COVID-19 in predicting complications of pulmonary recovery from mild or moderate COVID-19 is limited.
source: However, their applicability in predicting complications of pulmonary recovery from mild or moderate COVID-19 is limited.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a limitation of previously proposed risk factors.

claim: The results of univariate modeling, clustering, and ML prediction point towards a distinct long-term pulmonary risk phenotype that manifests during acute COVID-19 and early recovery and whose central components are protracted systemic (IL-6, CRP, anemia of inflammation) and microvascular inflammation (D-dimer), and strong humoral response (anti-S1/S2 IgG) demographic risk factors and comorbidities.
source: Our results of univariate modeling, clustering, and ML prediction point towards a distinct long-term pulmonary risk phenotype that manifests during acute COVID-19 and early recovery and whose central components are protracted systemic (IL-6, CRP, anemia of inflammation) and microvascular inflammation (D-dimer), and strong humoral response (anti-S1/S2 IgG) demographic risk factors and comorbidities (Sonnweber et al., 2020)⁠.
evidence: This statement summarizes the key findings of the study regarding risk phenotypes with a supporting citation.

claim: Consecutive monitoring of systemic inflammatory parameters analogous to concepts of interstitial lung disease in autoimmune disorders and anti-S1/S2 antibody levels may improve identification of the individuals at risk of chronic pulmonary damage irrespective of the acute COVID-19 severity.
source: Hence, consecutive monitoring of systemic inflammatory parameters analogous to concepts of interstitial lung disease in autoimmune disorders (Khanna et al., 2020) and anti-S1/S2 antibody levels may improve identification of the individuals at risk of chronic pulmonary damage irrespective of the acute COVID-19 severity.
evidence: This statement proposes a clinical implication based on study findings with a supporting citation.

claim: Clustering and ML have been employed for deep phenotyping and predicting acute and post-acute COVID-19 outcomes in multivariable data sets.
source: Clustering and ML have been employed for deep phenotyping and predicting acute and post-acute COVID-19 outcomes in multivariable data sets (Sahanic et al., 2021; Sudre et al., 2021a; Estiri et al., 2021; Demichev et al., 2021; Benito-León et al., 2021)⁠.
evidence: This statement cites published literature on the use of clustering and ML in COVID-19 research.

claim: Subsets of COVID-19 patients that significantly differ in the risk for long-term CT abnormalities may be defined by an easily accessible clinical parameter set available at the early post-COVID-19 assessment.
source: We demonstrate that subsets of COVID-19 patients that significantly differ in the risk for long-term CT abnormalities may be defined by an easily accessible clinical parameter set available at the early post-COVID-19 assessment.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding regarding patient stratification.

claim: The cluster classification correlated with the risk of long-term pulmonary abnormalities independently of the acute COVID-19 severity.
source: Furthermore, the cluster classification correlated with the risk of long-term pulmonary abnormalities independently of the acute COVID-19 severity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding regarding the independence of cluster classification.

claim: Technically unrelated ML classifiers and their ensemble trained without CT and LF explanatory variables can predict lung CT findings independently of their grading at the 6-month follow-up with good specificity and sensitivity in the training collective and CV.
source: We show that technically unrelated ML classifiers and their ensemble trained without CT and LF explanatory variables can predict lung CT findings independently of their grading at the 6-month follow-up with good specificity and sensitivity in the training collective and CV.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study finding regarding ML classifier performance.

claim: The limited sensitivity of ML classifiers at predicting moderate-to-severe CT abnormalities can be primarily traced back to their low frequency resulting in a suboptimal classifier training, especially in CV.
source: For the moderate-to-severe CT abnormalities, this can be primarily traced back to their low frequency resulting in a suboptimal classifier training, especially in CV.
evidence: This is a direct statement explaining the limited performance of ML classifiers for moderate-to-severe CT abnormalities.

claim: A substantial fraction of the participants (20.7%, n = 30) suffered from a preexisting respiratory condition (pulmonary disease, asthma, or COPD) likely paralleled by LF reduction, which possibly confounded the prediction of the post-COVID-19 LF deficits both by clustering and ML.
source: A substantial fraction of the participants (20.7%, n = 30) suffered from a preexisting respiratory condition (pulmonary disease, asthma, or COPD) likely paralleled by LF reduction, which possibly confounded the prediction of the post-COVID-19 LF deficits both by clustering and ML.
evidence: This statement identifies a potential confounding factor in the study with data on prevalence.

claim: Accumulating evidence suggests that post-acute COVID-19 symptoms are highly heterogeneous conditions with multiorgan, neurocognitive, and psychological manifestations, which may differ in risk factor constellations.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that post-acute COVID-19 symptoms are highly heterogeneous conditions with multiorgan, neurocognitive, and psychological manifestations (Sahanic et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Davis et al., 2021)⁠, which may differ in risk factor constellations.
evidence: This statement cites published literature on the heterogeneity of post-acute COVID-19 symptoms.

claim: The heterogeneity of post-acute COVID-19 symptoms could explain why univariate modeling, clustering, and ML failed to estimate persistent symptom risk in the small study cohort.
source: This could explain why univariate modeling, clustering, and ML failed to estimate persistent symptom risk in our small study cohort.
evidence: This statement provides an explanation for the limited performance of risk models for persistent symptoms.

claim: The ML prediction quality may greatly benefit from a larger training data set and inclusion of additional explanatory variables such as cellular readouts of inflammation, in-depth medication, and broader acute symptom data.
source: In general, the ML prediction quality may greatly benefit from a larger training data set and inclusion of additional explanatory variables such as cellular readouts of inflammation, in-depth medication, and broader acute symptom data.
evidence: This statement proposes potential improvements to ML prediction based on study limitations.

claim: The cluster- and ML classifiers represent resource-effective tools that may assist in the screening of medical record data and identification of COVID-19 patients requiring systematic CT and LF monitoring.
source: Nevertheless, the herein described cluster- and ML classifiers represent resource-effective tools that may assist in the screening of medical record data and identification of COVID-19 patients requiring systematic CT and LF monitoring.
evidence: This statement proposes a clinical application of the study findings.

claim: The clustering and prediction procedures were implemented in an open-source risk assessment application (https://im2-ibk.shinyapps.io/CovILD/).
source: To facilitate the identification of patients at risk for protracted respiratory recovery and enable validation in an external collective, we implemented the clustering and prediction procedures in an open-source risk assessment application (https://im2-ibk.shinyapps.io/CovILD/).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the implementation of study findings in a clinical tool.

claim: The study bears limitations primarily concerning the low sample size and the cross-sectional character of the trial.
source: Our study bears limitations primarily concerning the low sample size and the cross-sectional character of the trial.
evidence: This is a direct statement of study limitations.

claim: The impaired availability of the patients and the prolonged inpatient rehabilitation resulted in temporal overlap between the 60- and 100-day follow-up visits that may have impacted the accuracy of the longitudinal data.
source: Because of the impaired availability of the patients and the prolonged inpatient rehabiliation, the 60- and 100-day follow-up visits in part showed a temporal overlap that may have impacted the accuracy of the longitudinal data.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study limitation.

claim: Missingness of the consecutive outcome variable record and the participant dropout, particularly of mild and moderate COVID-19 cases, may have potentially confounded the participant clustering results and ML risk estimation for CT abnormalities and LF impairment since prolonged hospitalization was found to be a crucial cluster-defining and influential explanatory feature.
source: Missingness of the consecutive outcome variable record and the participant dropout, particularly of mild and moderate COVID-19 cases, may have also potentially confounded the participant clustering results and ML risk estimation for CT abnormalities and LF impairment since prolonged hospitalization was found to be a crucial cluster-defining and influential explanatory feature.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a study limitation and potential confounding factor.

claim: The reproducibility of the risk assessment algorithms was partially addressed by CV.
source: Additionally, even though the reproducibility of the risk assessment algorithms was partially addressed by CV, cluster and ML classifiers call for verification in a larger, independent multicenter collective of COVID-19 convalescents.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the validation approach used in the study.

claim: Cluster and ML classifiers call for verification in a larger, independent multicenter collective of COVID-19 convalescents.
source: Additionally, even though the reproducibility of the risk assessment algorithms was partially addressed by CV, cluster and ML classifiers call for verification in a larger, independent multicenter collective of COVID-19 convalescents.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the need for external validation of study findings.

claim: In the CovILD study cohort, there was a high frequency of CT and LF abnormalities and persistent symptoms at the 6-month follow-up, and a flattened recovery kinetics after 3 months post-COVID-19.
source: In summary, in our CovILD study cohort we found a high frequency of CT and LF abnormalities and persistent symptoms at the 6-month follow-up, and a flattened recovery kinetics after 3 months post-COVID-19.
evidence: This is a direct summary statement of key study findings.

claim: Systematic risk modeling revealed a set of clinical variables linked to protracted pulmonary recovery apart from the severity of acute infection such as inflammatory markers, anti-S1/S2 IgG levels, multimorbidity, and male sex.
source: Systematic risk modeling reveled a set of clinical variables linked to protracted pulmonary recovery apart from the severity of acute infection such as inflammatory markers, anti-S1/S2 IgG levels, multimorbidity, and male sex.
evidence: This is a direct summary statement of key study findings.

claim: Clustering and ML classifiers may help to identify individuals at risk of persistent lung lesions and to relocate medical resources to prevent long-term disability.
source: We demonstrate that clustering and ML classifiers may help to identify individuals at risk of persistent lung lesions and to relocate medical resources to prevent long-term disability.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the clinical implications of study findings.
